title: The Twelve-Factor App
notes: Factor names are from the published methodology. The `requirement` text is docket's plain statement of each factor's obligation, not a quotation; `citation` locates the factor so the original is one click away. Eleven of the twelve are answerable by reading a repository. Factor VIII is a property of how the app is deployed and scaled, so it is marked runtime and is never handed to an agent. Factor III is the one that overlaps security directly: config in the environment means secrets are not in the repository.

controls.title: Codebase — one codebase tracked in revision control, many deploys
controls.requirement: The application must be a single codebase under revision control, deployed to multiple environments, rather than several diverged copies or a codebase shared by multiple applications.
controls.evidence_hint: a single VCS root; vendored copies of a sibling service; environment-specific forks of the same module

controls.title: Dependencies — explicitly declare and isolate
controls.requirement: All dependencies must be declared completely and exactly in a manifest, and resolved into an isolated environment, so a build never relies on packages that happen to exist on the host.
controls.evidence_hint: requirements.txt / pyproject.toml / package.json present and pinned; a lockfile committed; unpinned or floating ranges; imports of packages that appear in no manifest

controls.title: Config — store config in the environment
controls.requirement: Everything that varies between deploys — credentials, hostnames, endpoints, feature toggles — must be read from the environment at runtime and must not be committed to the repository.
controls.evidence_hint: hardcoded API keys, passwords, tokens or connection strings; a committed .env with real values; config read via os.environ / process.env with a safe default; .env listed in .gitignore

controls.title: Backing services — treat as attached resources
controls.requirement: Databases, queues, caches and third-party services must be addressed by a URL or locator supplied in config, so one can be swapped for another without a code change.
controls.citation: The Twelve-Factor App, factor IV (Backing services)
controls.evidence_hint: DATABASE_URL-style config; hostnames or ports literal in code; a client constructed with an inline connection string

controls.title: Build, release, run — strictly separate stages
controls.requirement: The build stage must produce an immutable artifact, the release stage must combine it with config, and the run stage must not mutate code. Releases must be identifiable and not editable in place.
controls.citation: The Twelve-Factor App, factor V (Build, release, run)
controls.evidence_hint: a Dockerfile or CI pipeline producing a tagged artifact; a start command that installs dependencies or pulls code at boot; runtime writes into the application directory

controls.title: Processes — execute as stateless processes
controls.requirement: Application processes must be stateless and share nothing; any data that must persist belongs in a backing service, not in process memory or the local filesystem between requests.
controls.evidence_hint: module-level mutable dicts used as caches or sessions; local-filesystem session or upload storage; sticky-session assumptions

controls.title: Port binding — export services via port binding
controls.requirement: The application must be self-contained and export its service by binding a port supplied by the environment, rather than depending on a runtime injection into an external web server.
controls.citation: The Twelve-Factor App, factor VII (Port binding)
controls.evidence_hint: a port read from PORT with a sane default; a hardcoded bind port; reliance on being dropped into a servlet container or Apache module

controls.title: Concurrency — scale out via the process model
controls.requirement: The application must scale horizontally by running more processes of each type, with process types and their scaling declared rather than achieved by in-process threading tricks.

controls.title: Disposability — fast startup and graceful shutdown
controls.requirement: Processes must start quickly and shut down gracefully on SIGTERM: stop accepting new work, finish or requeue what is in flight, and release resources. Jobs must be safe to retry.
controls.evidence_hint: a SIGTERM handler or framework lifespan/shutdown hook; long blocking work started at import time; queue consumers that ack before the work completes

controls.title: Dev/prod parity — keep environments similar
controls.requirement: Development, staging and production must stay as alike as possible in backing-service types and versions, so behaviour observed in one predicts the others.
controls.citation: The Twelve-Factor App, factor X (Dev/prod parity)
controls.evidence_hint: sqlite in development against postgres in production; an in-memory queue or cache substituted locally; a docker-compose that mirrors production services

controls.title: Logs — treat logs as event streams
controls.requirement: The application must write its log stream unbuffered to stdout and must not manage log files, rotation or routing itself. Logs must not contain secrets or credentials.
controls.evidence_hint: logging configured to a file path or a rotating handler; print/console.log of request bodies, tokens or passwords; a logger that serialises whole request objects

controls.title: Admin processes — run admin tasks as one-off processes
controls.requirement: Migrations, backfills and console tasks must run as one-off processes against the same codebase and config as the running app, and must not be reachable as ordinary application endpoints.
controls.citation: The Twelve-Factor App, factor XII (Admin processes)
controls.evidence_hint: a migration or shell command exposed as an HTTP route; management commands that read a different config; a /debug or /admin/run endpoint invoking arbitrary tasks
